title: Character Analysis
description: Maggie, Willie, Hobson, Alice, Vickey, Albert Prosser, and Mrs Hepworth in depth.
content_html:
Character Analysis: An Overview

In the Edexcel exam, you must show detailed knowledge of character through AO1 (textual references) and AO4 (how Brighouse presents characters through language, structure, and dramatic methods). This lesson examines each major character, with key quotations and analysis of Brighouse’s methods.

Maggie Hobson

Maggie is the protagonist and the play’s moral centre. She is thirty years old, unmarried, and dismissed by her father as “shelved.” But Maggie is the most intelligent, capable, and determined character in the play. Her declaration “I’m a business woman” is both a statement of identity and a challenge to every assumption about what women can achieve.

Brighouse presents Maggie as a catalyst — she does not just respond to events; she creates them. She proposes to Willie, starts the business, negotiates the legal settlement, and dictates the final arrangement with Hobson. Her language is direct, practical, and unadorned: she says what she means without sentiment or hesitation. This concise speech style contrasts with Hobson’s bluster and the sisters’ fussy gentility.

Key Fact

Maggie’s key quotations: “I’m a business woman,” “I’ll tell you what I’ll do. I’ll take Willie Mossop,” and “I’m not a fool, Father.” Each shows her agency, intelligence, and refusal to accept patriarchal limitations.

Maggie anticipates the feminist movement by decades. She claims economic independence, chooses her own partner, and builds a business on equal partnership rather than male dominance. Yet Brighouse avoids making her a simple mouthpiece for women’s rights. Maggie is also pragmatic, occasionally ruthless, and not above manipulation. Her treatment of Willie in Act 1 — overriding his objections and physically removing Ada Figgins — shows a woman who knows what she wants and will not be deflected. This complexity makes her a compelling dramatic character rather than a political poster.

Willie Mossop

Willie undergoes the greatest transformation in the play. In Act 1, he is a timid, illiterate cellar worker who cannot look his employer’s daughter in the eye. By Act 4, he is the confident master of the business, insisting that the sign reads “Mossop & Hobson.” His journey from subservience to authority is the play’s central arc.

Willie’s language changes across the play, tracking his development. In Act 1, he speaks in short, hesitant phrases. By Act 4, he speaks in complete, confident sentences and even makes demands. His exclamation “By gum!” evolves from bewilderment to pride. “You told me to be strong and use the power that’s come to me” shows a man who understands his own growth and acknowledges Maggie’s role in it. Mrs Hepworth recognised his talent from the start: “You’re a natural born genius at making boots.”

Henry Horatio Hobson

Hobson is the antagonist, but Brighouse presents him with more complexity than a simple villain. He is a widower, a heavy drinker, and a stubborn patriarch who genuinely believes he knows best. His authority is built on the Victorian assumption that a father’s word is law — and when that assumption is challenged, he has nothing to fall back on.

Hobson is also a comic figure. His pompous speeches are constantly undercut by his actions: he lectures on respectability while stumbling home drunk; he claims business expertise while his shop fails. “Hobson, you’re a disgrace” sums up his trajectory from respected tradesman to helpless dependent. Yet the play does not destroy him. In the final scene, he is cared for by the daughter he undervalued — a resolution that is compassionate even as it is humiliating.

Key Fact

Hobson is a complex antagonist: comic in his pomposity, pitiable in his decline, and never truly villainous. Brighouse uses him to critique the patriarchal system rather than to demonise an individual.

Alice & Vickey

Maggie’s younger sisters serve as foils to her. Alice is concerned with respectability and social climbing; Vickey is the youngest and the most materialistic. Both want conventional marriages to professional men — Alice to Albert Prosser, Vickey to Fred Beenstock. They are embarrassed by Maggie’s choice of Willie and horrified by the humble wedding celebration.

Their function in the play is to represent what Maggie is not. They accept the rules of the class system and seek advancement within it; Maggie breaks the rules entirely. When Hobson needs care in Act 4, Alice and Vickey refuse — revealing that their genteel values do not extend to genuine family loyalty. They benefit from Maggie’s rebellion (receiving their settlements) without sharing her courage.

Albert Prosser & Mrs Hepworth

Albert Prosser is a solicitor’s son and Alice’s suitor. He represents the professional class that Alice aspires to join. In the early acts, he is a nervous, somewhat bumbling figure. His legal role in the trespass case against Hobson makes him a useful but unimpressive character — competent in his profession but lacking Maggie’s drive or Willie’s craft.

Mrs Hepworth appears briefly in Act 1 but her impact is enormous. As a wealthy, upper-class customer, her praise of Willie — “You’re a natural born genius at making boots” — carries authority that crosses class boundaries. She gives Willie her card and tells him to contact her if he ever leaves. This moment provides Maggie with the evidence she needs: Willie’s talent is objectively valuable, not just useful to Hobson’s shop. Mrs Hepworth represents a world where quality is recognised regardless of the maker’s social position — a meritocratic ideal that the play endorses.
exam_tip_html: When writing about character, always link to Brighouse’s methods (AO4). Don’t just describe what a character does — analyse how Brighouse presents them. For example: “Brighouse presents Willie’s transformation through his changing speech patterns — from monosyllabic hesitancy in Act 1 to confident, assertive sentences in Act 4 — dramatising his social mobility through language itself.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Maggie is the play’s protagonist and moral centre, defined by direct language, practical intelligence, and a refusal to accept patriarchal limitations.
  • Willie’s transformation — tracked through his changing speech — is the play’s central arc: from silent cellar worker to confident master.
  • Hobson is a complex comic antagonist whose decline critiques patriarchal complacency rather than demonising an individual.

practice_questions.text: How does Brighouse present Maggie Hobson as a woman who defies the expectations of her time? Refer to the whole play in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Perceptive analysis of Maggie across the play. Discusses: her proposal (gender role reversal), her business success (economic independence), her direct language style, her negotiation of the settlement, the contrast with Alice and Vickey. Victorian expectations of women, suffragette context. dialogue, foil characters, dramatic structure.
Top band (16-20): Clear analysis with relevant evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some explained points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Brighouse uses Willie Mossop’s changing language to dramatise his transformation from subservience to authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Sophisticated analysis of linguistic change as characterisation. Tracks: monosyllabic responses in Act 1, growing fluency in Act 2, confident demands in Act 4. Uses ‘By gum!’ as a motif. language as a method, speech patterns reflecting social position. class and education.
Top band (16-20): Clear tracking of language change with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic points.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: “Hobson is a comic character, but Brighouse also makes the audience feel sorry for him.” How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Balanced analysis of comedy and pathos. Comedy: pompous speeches undercut by behaviour, dramatic irony, physical comedy (trapdoor). Pathos: widower, genuine bewilderment at losing control, the dignity of his final acceptance. Brighouse’s dual presentation. patriarchal authority as system rather than personal failing.
Top band (16-20): Clear discussion of both aspects.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant analysis.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Brighouse use Alice and Vickey as foil characters to highlight Maggie’s qualities?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Perceptive contrast analysis. Alice/Vickey: conventional, status-conscious, snobbish, unwilling to sacrifice. Maggie: unconventional, practical, loyal, courageous. foil technique, the wedding scene as a key contrast. different models of womanhood in Victorian society.
Top band (16-20): Clear comparison.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some contrasts identified.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic comparison.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

practice_questions.text: Explore the significance of Mrs Hepworth’s role in the play. How does her brief appearance influence the plot and themes?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Perceptive analysis of a minor but pivotal character. Discusses: her recognition of Willie’s talent crossing class boundaries, the calling card as a plot device, her role as evidence for Maggie’s plan, the meritocratic ideal she represents. dramatic economy (brief appearance, large impact).
Top band (16-20): Clear analysis with textual support.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant points.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic response.
Lower band (1-5): Simple comments.

practice_questions.text: How does Brighouse present the relationship between Maggie and Willie as different from the other relationships in the play?
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (21-25) Perceptive comparison. Maggie/Willie: equal partnership, built on mutual skill, genuine growth. Alice/Albert and Vickey/Fred: conventional, status-driven, static. Hobson/his daughters: patriarchal control, exploitative. contrast between relationships as structural method. marriage as business arrangement vs partnership.
Top band (16-20): Clear comparison with evidence.
Upper-mid band (11-15): Some relevant contrasts.
Lower-mid band (6-10): Basic points.
Lower band (1-5): Minimal response.

glossary_terms.definition: A character whose actions drive the plot forward and who causes change in other characters and situations.
Describing speech or writing that is brief, clear, and to the point, without unnecessary words.
Lacking confidence and feeling that one is less important or capable than others.
The main character who opposes the protagonist, creating the central conflict of the narrative.
A character who contrasts with another character, highlighting particular qualities of each through the comparison.
A system in which people advance based on their abilities and talent rather than their wealth, family background, or social class.
